Ventilation: the process by which air moves in and out of the lung

Inspiration: an active process resulting from the contraction of inspiratory muscles

  • Diaphragm – innervated by phrenic nerves (C3-5); referred pain to shoulder and trapezius ridge
  • External intercostals – innervated by intercostal nerves
  • ↑ thoracic cavity volume, ↑ negative intrapleural pressure, lung expands, -1 mm Hg intrapulmonary pressure, AIR FLOWS IN

Expiration: a passive process resulting from the elastic recoil of the lung and chest wall to their equilibrium positions

  • Muscles of the abdominal wall (rectus abdominus, internal and external oblique muscles, transverse abdominus)
  • Internal intercostals
  • Becomes an active process during exercise and voluntary hyperventilation

Regulation of Respiration

Spontaneous respiration is produced by rhythmic discharges from the motor neurons that innervate the respiratory muscles

Voluntary control: can influence ventilation within limits; cerebral cortex → corticospinal tract → spinal neurons

Automatic control: ensures that blood PO2 and PCO2 are maintained in the normal range

  • Respiratory muscles – receive impulses from the controller
  • Central controller – coordinates and responds to the information provided by the receptors

Inspiratory area: dorsal medulla; inspiratory drive – inherent rhythmic excitability

  • o Pneumotaxic center: pons; limits the duration of the inspiratory drive – inhibits inspiration
  • o Apneustic center: lower pons; prevents termination of the inspiratory drive – stimulates inspiration
  • o Expiratory area: ventral medulla; dormant during normal quiet breathing – forced expiration
  • Receptors – collect information of the current status of blood gases and other factors

Central chemoreceptors: medulla; respond to changes in blood PCO2 (change in H+ concentration)

  • o Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid bodies, aortic bodies; respond to changes in blood PO2 (< 60 mm Hg = ↑ RR and VT)
  • o Lung receptors: pulmonary stretch receptors (overdistention = ↓ RR), irritant receptors (dust particles, cigarette smoke)
  • o Other receptors: receptors in the nose and upper airways (chemical and mechanical stimulation), joint and muscle
  • o receptors (exercise), pain and temperature receptors
  • Responses to changes in PaCO2 are rapid and sensitive – ↑ PaCO2 = ↑ ventilation; ↓ PaCO2 = ↓ ventilation
  • Responses to changes in PaO2 are less marked – important at high altitude and in certain clinical conditions
  • The combined effects of changes in PaCO2 and PaO2 can exceed the sum of the individual responses
  • During exercise, the arterial blood values of PCO2, PO2, and pH remain relatively constant

Asthma predictive index – children 1-3 years
  • ≥ 4 wheezing episodes (> 24 h) in the past year, with at least 1 physician-confirmed, + 1 major criterion or 2 minor criteria

  • Minor criteria: wheezing apart from colds; eosinophilia (≥ 4%); allergic sensitization to milk, egg, or peanuts
  • It is NOT a test for who has asthma now or who should be treated – predicts who will continue to wheeze into school age

Approach to Hemoptysis

Amount/rate of bleeding is variable: 100-650 mL over 24 hours; massive = 100 cc/hour

Pulmonary artery circulation = low-pressure system – supplies lung parenchyma

Bronchial artery circulation = high-pressure system – supplies bronchi and visceral pleura

1. Stabilize the patient: vitals, IV access, group/screen; reverse anticoagulation (tranexamic acid)

  • Position patient lateral decubitus, with bleeding side down
  • Use endotracheal tube to place an endobronchial blocker; ventilate elevated side
  • Manage bleeding with argon plasma coagulation or catheter embolization

2. Investigate the cause: CXR, chest CT, arteriography, bronchoscopy = gold standard (direct visualization, sampling, biopsy)

3. Treat the cause: neoplasm, bronchitis, bronchiectasis, pneumonia, pulmonary abscess, TB, pulmonary vasculitis (HHT)

blocks.html:
Deep vein thrombosis: blood clot within a deep vein (iliac, femoral, popliteal)

  • Virchow triad (SHE): stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial damage
  • Swelling, redness, warmth, pain
  • Ix: D-dimer test to rule out DVT; compression ultrasound with Doppler
  • Prophylaxis/acute Tx: unfractionated heparin, LMWH – enoxaparin
  • Tx/long-term prevention: direct oral anticoagulants – rivaroxaban, apixaban

Pulmonary emboli (PE): obstruction of the pulmonary artery or its branches by foreign material that originated elsewhere

  • Sudden-onset dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis
  • Ix: pulmonary angiography, ECG (sinus tachycardia)
  • Tx: anticoagulation – heparin, direct thrombin/factor Xa inhibitors

Anterior mediastinal masses (5 Ts): thyroid, thymus, thoracic aorta, terrible lymphoma, teratoma and germ cell tumours

Mesothelioma: cancer of the mesothelium in the lining of the lungs; may result in hemorrhagic pleural effusion or pleural thickening

  • Associated with inhaled asbestos; tobacco smoking is NOT a risk factor
Atelectasis: alveolar collapse
  • Obstructive: airway obstruction prevents new air from reaching distal airways – foreign body, mucus plug, tumor
  • Compressive: external compression decreases lung volumes – space-occupying lesion, pleural effusion
  • Contraction: scarring of lung parenchyma that distorts alveoli – sarcoidosis
  • Adhesive: lack of surfactant – NRDS in premature babies
Pleural effusion: excessive accumulation of fluid in the pleural space
  • Light’s criteria: pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5; pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH > 0.6, pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 upper

limit of normal serum LDH

  • Exudate: cloudy fluid (cellular) – infection, malignancy, connective tissue disease, lymphatic, trauma
  • Transudate: clear fluid (hypocellular) – ↑ hydrostatic pressure (HF, Na+ retention), ↓ oncotic pressure (cirrhosis)
  • Tx: serialthoracentesis, indwelling pleural catheter, chest tube and talc pleurodesis (irritant to try to stick lung to chest wall)
Pneumothorax: accumulation of air in the pleural space
  • Dyspnea, uneven chest expansion; chest pain, ↓ tactile fremitus, hyperresonance, diminished breath sounds on affected side
  • Primary spontaneous: rupture of apical subpleural bleb or cysts
  • Secondary spontaneous: diseased lung, mechanical ventilation with use of high pressures (barotrauma)
  • Traumatic: blunt (rib fracture), penetrating (gunshot), iatrogenic (central lung placement, lung biopsy, barotrauma)
  • Tension: any of the above; air enters the pleural space but cannot exit, increasing trapped air
  • Tx: needle decompression, chest tube placement

Pancoast tumour (superior sulcus tumour): carcinoma that occurs in the apex of the lung

  • May cause Pancoast syndrome by invading/compressing local structures – recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness), stellate

ganglion (Horner syndrome), SVC syndrome, brachiocephalic vein, brachial plexus, phrenic nerve (hemidiaphragm paralysis)

  • Tongue is larger in proportion to mouth
